messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is twenty-seven years old, single, and drives for a ride-share company in a Midwestern city. He came to therapy at the urging of his cousin, who found him sitting in his parked car at four in the morning, staring at the dashboard, after he had refused to take a fare because the passenger was wearing a wool coat. Marcus could not explain why the sight of that fabric—rough, dark, familiar—made his chest tighten and his hands go numb. He only knew that he had to get out of the car.

The memory that haunts him began when he was six years old, living with his father in a small apartment. His father was a man who believed in discipline delivered with a leather belt, and he had a specific way of approaching: slow, deliberate footsteps that Marcus learned to recognize from the kitchen, from the hallway, from anywhere in the house. The steps would stop behind him. Then the belt would come down across his back, his thighs, his arms. The leather was cold at first—the temperature of the room—but after a few swings it grew warm from friction and from Marcus’s own skin heat. He learned to brace for that particular warmth, the way it preceded the sting. He learned to hate the feel of the belt’s surface and the sound of footsteps that meant his father was done waiting.

Now, twenty-one years later, Marcus lives inside those sensations. The rough texture of a wool sleeve, the weight of a footstep too close behind him, the sudden warmth of a summer breeze on his arm—any of these can drop him straight back into the living room of his childhood. He has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. While driving, he constantly checks his rearview mirror, scanning for passengers who might lean forward too fast, for pedestrians who walk too near his door. He takes routes through high-crime neighborhoods at night not because they are faster, but because he tells himself he needs to stay sharp. The risky behavior—speeding through yellow lights, driving with a broken taillight, picking up riders in areas other drivers avoid—feels almost necessary, as though being reckless keeps him one step ahead of a danger he cannot name. Even when a passenger tells him, “You’re safe, man, just relax,” Marcus cannot believe it. Safety, for him, is an abstract word that has never matched what his body knows.

His body does not trust him. It reacts before his mind catches up: sweat on his palms, a racing heart, a freeze that makes him grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whiten. Marcus has come to believe that his body is his enemy, that it has permanently changed for the worse, that he is broken beyond repair. He avoids emotional closeness entirely. The few women he has dated ended things because he would not let them stay the night, would not let them touch his back, would not let them walk up behind him. He could not explain why. Instead he uses distraction—loud podcasts, constant phone scrolling, accepting back-to-back fares that keep him driving for ten hours straight. And when that fails, he smokes marijuana in his car between rides, telling himself it is the only way to stop the replay.

The cost of these strategies has been steep. He has lost touch with his mother’s side of the family, who live in a different state and who used to hold large gatherings every summer. He stopped going after his uncle accidentally brushed the back of his neck with a cold hand. He has no community, no church, no sense of belonging to the culture his parents came from. The isolation feels permanent, like a wall he built so long ago he cannot remember what was on the other side.

What finally brought Marcus to therapy was an accident. Last month, while driving a fare, a passenger dropped his phone on the floor. The sound—a sharp, close thud that Marcus heard as footsteps behind his seat—sent him into a flashback. He swerved, hit a curb, and ended up with a cracked rim and a panic attack that lasted forty minutes. He sat in the parking lot afterward, trembling, and called his cousin. Now he sits across from me, saying he does not know if talking can help, but he knows he cannot keep driving. He is most afraid that if he stops the hypervigilance, the danger will finally catch up. And he is hoping—barely—that maybe his body can learn a different way to feel safe.
